q: A pharmacy packs 1,000 tablets into bottles of 30. How many bottles can be filled, and how many tablets are left over?
w: 1,000 ÷ 30 = 33 R 10, because 30 × 33 = 990 and 1,000 - 990 = 10. So 33 full bottles with 10 tablets left over.

n.1: A remainder of 40 is larger than 30, so another bottle can still be filled.
n.2: 3 left over reads the decimal 33.33 as a remainder of 3; the remainder is 1,000 - 990 = 10 tablets.
n.3: 34 bottles would need 34 × 30 = 1,020 tablets, more than the 1,000 on hand.

q: A long division has a divisor of 13, a quotient of 47 and a remainder of 9. What is the dividend?
w: Dividend = quotient × divisor + remainder = 47 × 13 + 9 = 611 + 9 = 620. Check: 620 ÷ 13 = 47 R 9.

n.1: 611 is quotient × divisor but leaves out the remainder of 9.
n.2: 602 subtracts the remainder from 611 instead of adding it; the remainder is added back to quotient × divisor.
n.3: 600 drops the carried 2 in 47 × 3 (121 instead of 141), so 47 × 13 comes out as 591 before the 9 is added.

w: Zero divided by a nonzero number is 0, and a number divided by itself is 1: 0 + 1 = 1.

n.0: 0 treats 14 ÷ 14 as 0; a nonzero number divided by itself is 1.
n.1: Only division BY zero is undefined; 0 ÷ 14 has the zero in the dividend, so it equals 0.
n.3: 2 treats 0 ÷ 14 as 1; zero divided by 14 is 0.

q: Which expression is NOT equal to 24 × 15?
w: 24 × 15 = 360. The distributive property needs 24 to multiply BOTH parts of 10 + 5: 24 × 10 + 24 × 5 = 360. 24 × 10 + 5 = 245.

n.0: 24 × 10 + 24 × 5 = 240 + 120 = 360, a correct use of the distributive property.
n.3: 12 × 30 = 360: halving one factor and doubling the other keeps the product.

q: A pharmacy divides 6,120 tablets equally among 15 clinics. How many tablets does each clinic receive?
w: 61 ÷ 15 = 4 R 1. Bring down 2: 12 is smaller than 15, so write 0 in the quotient. Bring down 0: 120 ÷ 15 = 8. Answer 408. Check: 15 × 408 = 6,120.

n.0: 480 writes the zero at the end instead of in the tens place; 15 × 480 = 7,200.
n.1: 48 drops the 0 that belongs in the quotient when 12 is too small to divide by 15.
n.2: 4,080 adds an extra zero; 15 × 4,080 = 61,200.

q: A blood bank collected 1,487 units in May, 2,056 in June and 968 in July. How many units did it collect in all?
w: Ones: 7 + 6 + 8 = 21, write 1, carry 2. Tens: 8 + 5 + 6 + 2 = 21, write 1, carry 2. Hundreds: 4 + 0 + 9 + 2 = 15, write 5, carry 1. Thousands: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Total 4,511.

n.0: 3,543 adds only May and June and leaves out July.
n.1: 3,511 forgets the 1 carried into the thousands place.
n.3: 4,501 carries 1 instead of 2 from the ones column (21).

q: A nurse works three 12-hour shifts each week. How many hours does she work in a year of 52 weeks if she takes 4 weeks of vacation?
w: Hours per week: 3 × 12 = 36. Weeks worked: 52 - 4 = 48. Hours: 36 × 48 = 1,728.

n.0: 1,872 counts all 52 weeks and leaves out the 4 weeks of vacation.
n.2: 1,868 subtracts 4 hours instead of 4 weeks of shifts (36 × 52 - 4).
n.3: 576 counts one 12-hour shift a week (12 × 48) instead of three.

q: A 100 mL bag of solution is divided equally into 8 syringes. How many milliliters go into each syringe?
w: 100 ÷ 8 = 12 R 4. As a decimal the remainder is 4/8 = 0.5, so each syringe gets 12.5 mL. Check: 8 × 12.5 = 100.

n.0: 1.25 mL places the decimal point one place too far left; 8 × 1.25 = 10, not 100.
n.2: 12.04 mL writes the remainder 4 in the hundredths place; the remainder is 4/8 of a milliliter.
n.3: 12.4 mL writes the remainder 4 as the decimal digits; 4 left over out of 8 is 0.5, not 0.4.

q: Evaluate 18 - 6 ÷ 3 × 2 + 4.
w: Multiplication and division have equal rank, so work left to right: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, then 2 × 2 = 4. Then add and subtract left to right: 18 - 4 = 14, and 14 + 4 = 18.

n.0: 12 works strictly left to right from the start (18 - 6 first), ignoring that division and multiplication come before subtraction.
n.1: 21 multiplies 3 × 2 before dividing (6 ÷ 6 = 1); division comes first here because it is on the left.
n.3: 10 adds 4 + 4 before subtracting; addition and subtraction are done left to right.

q: Evaluate 40 ÷ (2 + 3) × 4 - 3². Enter the number only.
w: Parentheses: 2 + 3 = 5. Exponent: 3² = 9. Division and multiplication left to right: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, then 8 × 4 = 32. Subtraction: 32 - 9 = 23.

q: Evaluate -4² + (-2)³.
w: In -4² the exponent applies only to 4: -(4 × 4) = -16. In (-2)³ the parentheses include the sign: (-2)(-2)(-2) = -8. Sum: -16 + (-8) = -24.

n.0: 8 treats -4² as (-4)² = 16, then adds -8.
n.1: -8 treats (-2)³ as +8 (an odd number of negative factors is negative), giving -16 + 8.
n.2: -22 treats (-2)³ as -2 × 3 = -6; the exponent means multiplying -2 by itself three times.

q: What is the value of the expression (8 - 2 × 5)² ÷ 4 + 6?
w: Inside the parentheses, multiply first: 2 × 5 = 10, so 8 - 10 = -2. Square: (-2)² = 4. Divide: 4 ÷ 4 = 1. Add: 1 + 6 = 7.

n.0: 5 squares -2 as -4; a negative number squared is positive.
n.1: 0.4 adds 4 + 6 before dividing; division comes before addition.
n.3: 231 works left to right inside the parentheses ((8 - 2) × 5 = 30), then 900 ÷ 4 + 6.

w: Parentheses: 3 - 7 = -4. Multiply: -2 × (-4) = 8. Subtracting a negative is adding: 8 - (-5) = 8 + 5 = 13.

n.0: 3 treats - (-5) as -5 instead of +5 (8 - 5).
n.1: -8 distributes -2 to the 3 only: -6 - 7 + 5.
n.2: -3 gives -2 × (-4) a negative sign (-8 + 5); the product of two negatives is positive.

q: Evaluate 36 ÷ 4 × 3 - 2².
w: Exponent: 2² = 4. Divide and multiply left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, 9 × 3 = 27. Subtract: 27 - 4 = 23.

n.0: -1 multiplies 4 × 3 before dividing (36 ÷ 12 - 4); division is on the left, so it goes first.
n.1: 9 subtracts 3 - 2 before squaring and multiplying; subtraction comes last.
n.2: 625 works left to right and squares last: (27 - 2)².

q: Evaluate 50 - 2 × (3 + 4)².
w: Parentheses: 3 + 4 = 7. Exponent: 7² = 49. Multiply: 2 × 49 = 98. Subtract: 50 - 98 = -48.

n.0: -146 multiplies 2 × 7 before squaring: 50 - 14²; the exponent comes before multiplication.
n.1: 2,352 subtracts 50 - 2 first: 48 × 49; multiplication comes before subtraction.
n.2: 0 squares each term inside the parentheses (9 + 16 = 25) instead of squaring the sum 7.

w: Each set of parentheses first: 18 + 6 = 24 and 4 × 2 = 8. Divide: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. Add: 3 + 5 = 8.

n.0: 3 is the quotient before the final + 5 is done.
n.1: 17 drops the parentheses around 4 × 2 and works 24 ÷ 4 × 2 + 5 = 12 + 5.
n.3: 26 drops all parentheses: 18 + 6 ÷ 4 × 2 + 5 = 18 + 3 + 5.

q: A clinic receives 5 boxes of 24 syringes and 3 boxes of 12 syringes, then uses 40 syringes. Which expression gives the number of syringes left?
w: Each box count multiplies its own box size, the products are added, and the 40 used is subtracted: 5 × 24 + 3 × 12 - 40 = 120 + 36 - 40 = 116.

n.1: (5 × 24 + 3) × 12 adds the 3 boxes as if they were syringes, then multiplies everything by 12: 123 × 12 - 40 = 1,436.
n.2: (5 + 3) × (24 + 12) treats all 8 boxes as holding 36 syringes each (288 - 40 = 248).
n.3: 5 × (24 + 3 × 12) multiplies the 3 boxes of 12 by 5 as well, giving 5 × 60 - 40 = 260.

q: Evaluate 4 + 12 × 4 - 8 ÷ 2.
w: Multiply and divide first: 12 × 4 = 48 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Then add and subtract left to right: 4 + 48 - 4 = 48.

n.0: 22 divides the whole sum by 2: (4 + 48 - 8) ÷ 2.
n.2: 28 works strictly left to right, as a basic calculator does: ((4 + 12) × 4 - 8) ÷ 2.
n.3: -20 subtracts 4 - 8 before multiplying: 4 + 12 × (-4) ÷ 2.

w: Innermost first: 4 + 2 = 6, and 6² = 36. Brackets: 20 - 36 = -16. Then 3 × (-16) = -48, and -48 ÷ 4 = -12.

n.0: 0 squares each term separately (16 + 4 = 20), so the brackets become 20 - 20.
n.1: -48 is 3 × (-16), one step short: the division by 4 has not been done.
n.3: 51 multiplies only the 20 by 3 and divides only the 36 by 4: 60 - 9.

w: Parentheses: 5 - 9 = -4. Multiply: -3 × (-4) = 12. Divide: 12 ÷ (-4) = -3. Subtract: 12 - (-3) = 12 + 3 = 15.

n.0: 9 makes 12 ÷ (-4) positive (12 - 3); a positive divided by a negative is negative.
n.2: -9 gives -3 × (-4) a negative sign (-12 + 3); two negatives multiply to a positive.
n.3: 0 subtracts 12 - 12 before dividing by -4; division comes before subtraction.

q: At 6 a.m. the outdoor temperature in Fargo was -7°F. By noon it had risen 15 degrees, and by 9 p.m. it had fallen 11 degrees from the noon reading. What was the temperature at 9 p.m.?
w: Start at -7, add the rise and subtract the fall: -7 + 15 = 8, then 8 - 11 = -3°F.

n.0: 11°F treats the starting temperature as +7 (7 + 15 - 11).
n.1: 19°F adds the 11-degree fall instead of subtracting it (8 + 11).
n.2: 3°F drops the negative sign; 8 - 11 is 3 below zero.

q: What is the value of (-3) × 4 × (-2) × (-1) ÷ (-6)?
w: Multiply left to right: (-3)(4) = -12; (-12)(-2) = 24; (24)(-1) = -24. Then -24 ÷ (-6) = 4. There are four negative signs (an even number), so the result is positive.

n.0: -4 miscounts the negative signs; there are four negatives, an even number, so the result is positive.
n.1: 144 multiplies -24 by -6 instead of dividing.
n.2: -144 multiplies by -6 instead of dividing and also miscounts the signs.

q: A scuba diver is 42 feet below the surface (-42 ft). She swims to a depth of 17 feet below the surface (-17 ft). Which describes the change in her position?
w: Change = final - initial = -17 - (-42) = -17 + 42 = 25. A positive change means she rose 25 feet.

n.0: 59 adds the depths, and the direction is also wrong; -17 is closer to the surface.
n.1: The change is positive (-17 is above -42), so she moved up, not down.
n.2: 59 adds the two depths (42 + 17) instead of finding the difference.

q: Darius's checking account was overdrawn, with a balance of -$37. He deposited $300 and then paid two bills of $84.50 and $128.50. What is his balance now? Enter the amount in whole dollars.

tr.124: Treated the starting balance as +$37 instead of -$37.
tr.263: Stopped after the deposit and did not subtract the two bills.

q: A hiker starts at a point 135 feet below sea level. She climbs 420 feet and then descends 190 feet. Where does she end up relative to sea level?
w: Write the start as -135. Then -135 + 420 - 190 = 285 - 190 = 95. A positive result is above sea level: 95 ft above.

n.0: 365 treats the starting point as +135 instead of -135.
n.1: 475 adds the 190-foot descent instead of subtracting it.
n.3: The result, +95, is positive, so she is above sea level.

q: A freezer reads -18°C. During a power outage it warms 2°C each hour for 5 hours, then cools 3°C each hour for 3 hours. What does it read then?
w: Warming adds and cooling subtracts: -18 + 5 × 2 - 3 × 3 = -18 + 10 - 9 = -17°C.

n.0: -19°C adds one 2°C rise and one 3°C drop (-18 + 2 - 3) instead of 5 rises and 3 drops.
n.1: 19°C drops the negative sign on the start (18 + 10 - 9).
n.3: -37°C treats the warming as cooling (-18 - 10 - 9).

q: Which expression has a negative value?
w: -4² means -(4 × 4) = -16, which is negative. The exponent applies only to 4, not to the negative sign.

n.1: (-4)² = 16; the parentheses include the sign, and two negative factors give a positive.
n.2: (-2)³ = -8, and -8 × (-3) = 24, which is positive.
n.3: -3 × (-5) = 15; two negatives multiply to a positive.

q: One patient's dressing is changed every 4 days and another's IV site every 6 days. Both were done today. In how many days will both next fall on the same day?
w: The next shared day is the least common multiple of 4 and 6. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12; multiples of 6: 6, 12. LCM = 12 days.

n.0: 2 is the greatest common factor of 4 and 6, not the least common multiple.
n.1: 10 adds the two intervals; the schedules meet at a common multiple.
n.3: 24 multiplies 4 × 6, a common multiple but not the least; both fall together on day 12 first.

q: The value of √90 lies between which pair of numbers?
w: 9² = 81 and 10² = 100. Since 81 < 90 < 100, √90 is between 9 and 10 (about 9.49).

n.0: 9² = 81, which is already less than 90, so √90 is greater than 9.
n.1: 81 and 100 are the perfect squares on either side of 90; √90 itself is about 9.49, which lies between their square roots, 9 and 10.
n.2: 10² = 100, which is already greater than 90, so √90 is less than 10.

q: Evaluate 5² + 3 × 2³ - √64. Enter the number only.
w: Exponents and roots first: 5² = 25, 2³ = 8 and √64 = 8. Multiply: 3 × 8 = 24. Then add and subtract left to right: 25 + 24 - 8 = 41.

q: What is √0.81?

n.0: 0.405 is 0.81 ÷ 2; a square root is not half the number.
n.1: 0.09 × 0.09 = 0.0081, not 0.81; the decimal places were miscounted.
n.2: 0.6561 is 0.81², the square, not the square root.

q: Which number is prime?
w: 53 has exactly two factors, 1 and 53: it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7 (7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64, so no larger prime needs checking).

n.0: 91 = 7 × 13, so it is composite.
n.1: 57 = 3 × 19 (digit sum 12 is divisible by 3), so it is composite.
n.3: 51 = 3 × 17 (digit sum 6 is divisible by 3), so it is composite.

q: A lab balance displays the mass of a sample as 47.0652 grams. The lab report requires masses rounded to the nearest hundredth of a gram. What mass should be reported?
w: The hundredths digit is 6. The digit to its right (thousandths) is 5, so round up: 47.0652 → 47.07 g.

n.0: 47.065 g rounds to the nearest thousandth.
n.2: 47.1 g rounds to the nearest tenth, not the nearest hundredth.
n.3: 47.06 g truncates; the next digit is 5, so the hundredths digit rounds up.

q: A regional hospital system reported serving 248,513 patients last year. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
w: The ten-thousands digit is 4 (in 248,513). The digit to its right is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up: 250,000.

n.0: 200,000 is rounded to the nearest hundred thousand.
n.1: 249,000 is rounded to the nearest thousand.
n.3: 240,000 truncates; the thousands digit 8 means rounding up.

q: A dosage calculation gives a volume of 3.96 mL, and the syringe being used is marked in tenths of a milliliter. What is 3.96 rounded to the nearest tenth? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.3.1: Rounded the 9 up to 10 but did not carry the 1 into the ones place.

w: The tenths digit is 9. The hundredths digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 9 rounds up to 10, carrying 1 into the ones place: 3.96 → 4.0 mL (entered as 4).

q: A hospital department logged 2,749.5 overtime hours last year. What is 2,749.5 rounded to the nearest hundred?
w: The hundreds digit is 7. Look only at the digit to its right (tens), which is 4, so keep 7: 2,700.

n.0: 2,800 rounds in two steps (2,749.5 → 2,750 → 2,800). Round once, using the tens digit.
n.2: 2,750 rounds to the nearest ten, not the nearest hundred.
n.3: 3,000 rounds to the nearest thousand.

q: In the number 52.0847, which digit is in the thousandths place?
w: Right of the point: 0 tenths, 8 hundredths, 4 thousandths, 7 ten-thousandths. The thousandths digit is 4.

n.0: 0 is in the tenths place, the first place after the point.
n.2: 7 is in the ten-thousandths place, the fourth place after the point.
n.3: 8 is in the hundredths place, the second place after the point.

q: Which is the correct way to write 6.045 in words?
o: six and four hundred five thousandths
w: Read the digits after the point as a whole number (045 = forty-five) and name the place of the last digit (thousandths): six and forty-five thousandths.

n.1: Four hundred five thousandths is 6.405; the 0 comes right after the point in 6.045.
n.2: Forty-five ten-thousandths is 6.0045, one place too far right.
n.3: Forty-five hundredths is 6.45; the last digit of 6.045 is in the thousandths place.

q: Which number is three hundred six and twelve thousandths?
w: Three hundred six = 306. Twelve thousandths must end in the thousandths place (third place): 0.012. Together: 306.012.

n.0: 306.0012 is twelve ten-thousandths, one place too far right.
n.1: 36.012 drops the zero in the tens place of three hundred six.
n.3: 306.12 is twelve hundredths, not twelve thousandths.

q: A county reports 1,349,506 residents. What is this number rounded to the nearest hundred thousand?
w: The hundred-thousands digit is 3. The digit to its right is 4, so keep the 3 and zero the rest: 1,300,000.

n.0: 1,400,000 rounds in stages (1,349,506 to 1,350,000 to 1,400,000); only the digit right after the target place counts.
n.1: 1,000,000 rounds to the nearest million.
n.2: 1,350,000 rounds to the nearest ten thousand.

q: A lab result of 2.0448 mmol/L must be reported to the nearest hundredth. What value is reported?
w: The hundredths digit is 4. The digit right after it is 4, which is 4 or less, so keep it: 2.04.

n.0: 2.0 rounds to the nearest tenth.
n.1: 2.045 rounds to the nearest thousandth.
n.2: 2.05 rounds in stages (2.0448 to 2.045 to 2.05); only the thousandths digit decides.

q: Which number has 3 in the thousands place and 7 in the hundredths place?
w: In 3,815.27 the 3 is in the thousands place and the 7 is two places right of the point, the hundredths place.

n.0: In 1,385.27 the 3 is in the hundreds place.
n.2: In 7,815.23 the two digits are swapped: 7 thousands and 3 hundredths.
n.3: In 3,815.72 the 7 is in the tenths place, the first place after the point.

q: A vial contains 5 mL of medication. A nurse withdraws 1.25 mL for one patient and then 0.8 mL for a second patient. How much medication is left in the vial?
w: Line up the decimal points. Amount withdrawn: 1.25 + 0.80 = 2.05 mL. Amount left: 5.00 - 2.05 = 2.95 mL.

n.0: 3.75 mL subtracts only the first withdrawal.
n.1: 3.67 mL treats 0.8 as 0.08 (lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points), so only 1.33 mL is subtracted.
n.3: 2.05 mL is the total withdrawn, not the amount left.

q: A patient on a fluid restriction weighed 68.4 kg on Monday and 67.85 kg on Friday. How many kilograms did the patient lose between the two weigh-ins? Enter the number of kilograms only.

n.2: 17.036 forgets the 1 carried from the tenths column into the ones.
n.3: 20.34 reads 0.256 as 2.56, shifting its digits one place left.

n.1: 18.457 subtracts only the whole numbers (30 - 12) and keeps the .457.

q: How much greater is 5.3 than 4.87?

q: An account holds $412.50. A deposit of $86.25 is made, then payments of $129.40 and $57.08 clear. What is the balance?

q: A 9.06 g sample loses 3.9 g of water when it is dried. What mass remains?
w: Write 3.9 as 3.90 and line up the points: 9.06 - 3.90. Hundredths 6 - 0 = 6; tenths borrow: 10 - 9 = 1; ones 8 - 3 = 5. Answer 5.16 g.

n.0: 8.67 g lines up the last digits, subtracting 0.39 instead of 3.9.
n.1: 6.16 g forgets to reduce the ones digit from 9 to 8 after borrowing.
n.3: 6.96 g takes the smaller digit from the larger in the tenths column (9 - 0) instead of borrowing.

q: Three lab samples must total 10 g. Two of them weigh 3.75 g and 4.6 g. What must the third sample weigh?

n.0: 2.65 g forgets to reduce the ones digit after borrowing in 10.00 - 8.35.

q: Each tablet of a medication contains 0.125 mg of the active drug. A patient takes 2.5 tablets each day. How many milligrams of the drug does the patient take each day?
w: Multiply: 125 × 25 = 3,125. The factors have 3 + 1 = 4 decimal places in total, so the product is 0.3125 mg.

q: A cafeteria worker pours a 6.3-liter container of soup into bowls that each hold 0.18 liter. How many bowls can be filled?
w: Move both decimal points 2 places right so the divisor is a whole number: 6.3 ÷ 0.18 = 630 ÷ 18 = 35 bowls.

n.3: 3.5 moves the decimal point in 0.18 two places but in 6.3 only one place.

q: A clinic orders 24 boxes of exam gloves listed at $8.75 per box. The supplier takes $0.50 off the price of each box. What is the total cost of the order?

q: A lab technician multiplies two measurements and gets a product of 0.0024. Which multiplication gives a product of exactly 0.0024?

q: A 12-pack of bottled water costs $5.40, and a 30-pack of the same bottles costs $12.90. How much less per bottle does the 30-pack cost than the 12-pack?

q: A pharmacy has 0.6 g of a powdered drug. Each dose uses 0.003 g. How many doses can be prepared from the powder?
w: Move both decimal points 3 places right: 0.6 ÷ 0.003 = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 doses.

q: A 0.45-liter bottle of hand sanitizer costs $3.15. At this price, what is the cost per liter of hand sanitizer?
w: Cost per liter = price ÷ liters: $3.15 ÷ 0.45 = 315 ÷ 45 = $7.00 per liter.

n.0: $1.42 multiplies $3.15 by 0.45 (1.4175) instead of dividing.

n.3: $0.14 divides 0.45 by 3.15, which gives liters per dollar.

w: Move both points 1 place right so the divisor is whole: 0.72 ÷ 9 = 0.08. Check: 0.08 × 0.9 = 0.072.

n.0: 0.8 moves the dividend's point 2 places while the divisor's moved 1.
n.1: 0.008 moves the divisor's point but not the dividend's (0.072 ÷ 9).
n.2: 8 divides 72 by 9 and loses track of the decimal point altogether.

q: A patient takes 0.25 mg of a drug 3 times a day for 14 days. How many milligrams does the patient take in all?

n.0: 31.5 mg multiplies by 3 twice: the daily 0.75 mg already includes the 3 doses.
n.1: 3.5 mg counts one dose a day (0.25 × 14).
n.2: 1.05 mg places the decimal point one place too far left in 0.75 × 14.

q: At a pharmacy, Ana buys 3 bottles of vitamins at $4.79 each and 2 boxes of bandages at $12.65 each. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change should she receive?

n.0: $22.98 multiplies the vitamins by 3 but counts only one box of bandages.
n.1: $39.67 is the total cost, not the change.
n.2: $32.56 subtracts one bottle and one box ($4.79 + $12.65) instead of the full quantities.

q: Mia earns $18.40 per hour for her first 40 hours each week and 1.5 times that rate for every hour over 40. Last week she worked 46.5 hours. What was her total pay?

n.0: $1,283.40 pays all 46.5 hours at the overtime rate.
n.1: $855.60 pays all 46.5 hours at the regular rate.
n.2: $901.60 counts only 6 overtime hours instead of 6.5.

q: A nursing program needs lab coats for 150 students and 8 instructors. It already has 10 new coats in storage, and more coats come only in boxes of 12. What is the least number of boxes the program must order so that everyone gets a coat?
w: Coats needed: 150 + 8 = 158. Subtract the 10 in storage: 158 - 10 = 148. Boxes: 148 ÷ 12 = 12.33. Twelve boxes hold only 144 coats, so round up to 13 boxes (156 coats, enough for the 148 still needed).

n.0: 12 boxes rounds 12.33 down; 12 boxes plus storage give 144 + 10 = 154 coats, 4 short.
n.1: 11 boxes subtracts the 8 instructors instead of adding them (150 - 8 - 10 = 132, and 132 ÷ 12 = 11).
n.3: 14 boxes ignores the 10 coats in storage (158 ÷ 12 = 13.17, rounded up), so it orders one box too many.

q: A clinic buys 38 boxes of syringes at $19.75 per box. Rounding each number to the nearest ten, which is the estimate of the total cost?
w: 38 rounds to 40 and $19.75 rounds to $20. Estimate: 40 × $20 = $800. (The exact cost is $750.50.)

n.0: $400 rounds $19.75 down to $10; the ones digit 9 means rounding up to $20.
n.1: $300 truncates both numbers (30 × $10) instead of rounding.
n.2: $600 rounds 38 down to 30; the ones digit 8 means rounding up to 40.

q: A prescriber orders 0.15 mg of a drug for each kilogram of body weight. The patient weighs 72.6 kg. What is the dose? Do not round until the final answer, and round it to the nearest tenth of a milligram. Enter the number only.

tr.11: Rounded the weight to 73 kg first (0.15 × 73 = 10.95, which rounds to 11.0).

w: Dose = 0.15 × 72.6 = 10.89 mg. Round only at the end: the hundredths digit is 9, so 10.89 → 10.9 mg.

q: A multidose vial contains 20 mL of medication, and 4.5 mL has already been drawn from it. Each dose is 1.5 mL. How many more full doses can be drawn from the vial?
w: Medication left: 20 - 4.5 = 15.5 mL. Doses: 15.5 ÷ 1.5 = 10.33. Only complete doses count, so round down: 10 full doses (10 × 1.5 = 15 mL; 0.5 mL is left over).

n.1: 14 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn and also rounds 13.33 up instead of down.
n.2: 11 rounds 10.33 up; 11 doses would need 16.5 mL, but only 15.5 mL is left.
n.3: 13 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn (20 ÷ 1.5 = 13.33, rounded down).

q: To estimate 6.8 × 4.6, a student rounds both numbers to the nearest whole number and calculates 7 × 5 = 35. How does this estimate compare with the exact product?
o: An exact estimate, because the rounding errors are both less than 0.5
An underestimate, because 4.6 was rounded more than 6.8
An overestimate by 0.6, the total amount the factors were rounded up
An overestimate, because both factors were rounded up
w: Both factors were rounded up (6.8 → 7 and 4.6 → 5), so the estimate is too high. Exact: 6.8 × 4.6 = 31.28, so 35 is 3.72 too high.

n.0: The rounding errors are small, but they still change the product (35 vs 31.28).
n.1: Rounding both factors up makes the product larger, so the estimate is too high, not too low.
n.2: The round-offs are multiplied by the other factors, so the error is 35 - 31.28 = 3.72, not 0.6.

q: A travel nurse worked 38.5, 41.2, 39.8, 40.6 and 39.1 hours over five weeks. Which is the best estimate of the total number of hours she worked?
w: All five values cluster near 40, so estimate 5 × 40 = 200 hours. (Exact: 199.2 hours.)

n.0: 160 counts four weeks (4 × 40) instead of five.
n.2: 220 rounds every value up to the next ten (40 + 50 + 40 + 50 + 40) instead of to the nearest ten.
n.3: 170 truncates each value to the tens place (30 + 40 + 30 + 40 + 30) instead of rounding.

q: Three coworkers split a $47.83 lunch bill equally. Each person's share is rounded up to the next cent so that the bill is fully covered. How much does each person pay?
w: $47.83 ÷ 3 = $15.9433... Rounding up to the next cent gives $15.95. Check: 3 × $15.95 = $47.85, which covers the bill.

n.0: $16.00 rounds up to the next dollar, not the next cent.
n.2: $15.90 rounds down to the nearest ten cents and leaves the bill short.
n.3: $15.94 is ordinary rounding; 3 × $15.94 = $47.82, which is 1 cent short.

q: During a shift, a patient drinks 240 mL of water, 180 mL of juice, 2 cups of tea that hold 120 mL each, and half of a 500 mL bottle of an oral supplement. What is the patient's total oral intake? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.790: Counted only one cup of tea.
tr.1160: Counted the whole 500 mL bottle instead of half.

q: A 24-ounce bag of brown rice costs $4.56. A 2.5-pound bag of the same rice costs $7.20. Which bag costs less per ounce, and by how much?
w: 24-oz bag: $4.56 ÷ 24 = $0.19 per ounce. 2.5-lb bag: 2.5 × 16 = 40 oz, and $7.20 ÷ 40 = $0.18 per ounce. The 2.5-lb bag is cheaper by $0.19 - $0.18 = $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This reverses the comparison; $0.18 per ounce is less than $0.19 per ounce.
n.2: $2.64 compares the bag prices, not the price per ounce.
n.3: $0.10 per ounce uses 1 lb = 10 oz (25 oz in the bag); 1 lb = 16 oz.

q: A home health nurse drives 24 miles at an average of 32 miles per hour to reach her first patient, then 35 miles at 60 miles per hour to reach her second. What is her total driving time?
w: Time = distance ÷ speed. Leg 1: 24 ÷ 32 = 0.75 h = 45 min. Leg 2: 35 ÷ 60 = 7/12 h = 35 min. Total: 45 + 35 = 80 min = 1 h 20 min.

n.0: 1 h 33 min reads 1.33 hours as 1 hour 33 minutes; 0.33 h is about 20 minutes.
n.1: 1 h 17 min divides the total distance by the average of the two speeds (59 ÷ 46); the legs must be timed separately.
n.3: 45 min is the time for the first leg only.

q: Lin buys 3 scrub tops at $24.50 each and 2 pairs of scrub pants at $19.75 each. She uses a coupon for $10 off her total purchase and pays with $150. How much change should she receive? Enter the amount in dollars.

q: A community clinic saw 1,248 patients in the first quarter of the year and 1,575 in the second quarter. Its goal for the first half of the year was 3,000 patients. How many more patients would the clinic have needed to meet its goal?
w: Patients seen: 1,248 + 1,575 = 2,823. Shortfall: 3,000 - 2,823 = 177 patients.

n.0: 327 is how many more patients were seen in the second quarter than in the first.
n.1: 2,823 is the number of patients seen, not the number still needed.
n.2: 1,425 subtracts only the second quarter's patients from the goal.

q: A 1,000 mL IV bag infuses at 125 mL per hour for 3.5 hours, then at 75 mL per hour for 2.5 hours. How many milliliters remain in the bag? Enter the number only.

tr.250: Used 125 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.550: Used 75 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.625: Gave the volume infused instead of the volume remaining.

q: A patient must take 2 tablets three times a day for 14 days and already has 25 of these tablets at home. More tablets are sold only in bottles of 30. How many bottles must be purchased to complete the full course?
w: Tablets needed: 2 × 3 × 14 = 84. Subtract the 25 at home: 84 - 25 = 59. Bottles: 59 ÷ 30 = 1.97. One bottle is not enough, so round up to 2 bottles (60 tablets, enough for the 59 still needed).

n.0: 1 bottle rounds 1.97 down; 30 + 25 = 55 tablets would run out before the 84 needed.
n.1: 3 bottles ignores the 25 tablets at home (84 ÷ 30 = 2.8, rounded up), so it buys one bottle too many.
n.2: 4 bottles adds the 25 tablets at home to the 84 needed (109 ÷ 30 = 3.63) instead of subtracting them.

q: A bottle holds 250 mL of a liquid medication. The prescribed dose is 7.5 mL twice a day. How many full days will the bottle last?
w: Daily use: 7.5 × 2 = 15 mL. Days: 250 ÷ 15 = 16.67. Only complete days count, so round down to 16 days (16 × 15 = 240 mL).

n.0: This rounds 16.67 up. After 16 days only 10 mL is left, which is not enough for both doses on day 17.
n.1: This is the number of full doses (250 ÷ 7.5), not days; there are 2 doses per day.
n.2: This rounds the number of doses (33.3) up and treats each dose as a day.

q: A clinic can buy exam gloves in a box of 100 for $8.40 or in a case of 10 such boxes for $76.50. How much is saved per glove by buying the case instead of single boxes?
w: Single box: $8.40 ÷ 100 = $0.084 per glove. Case: $76.50 ÷ 1,000 = $0.0765 per glove. Savings: 0.084 - 0.0765 = $0.0075 per glove, which is 0.75 cent.

n.1: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 cent; this moves the decimal one place too far.
n.2: This is the savings per box of 100 gloves ($8.40 - $7.65), not per glove.
n.3: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 of a cent, not 7.5 cents.
